beats.text: This is me losing six hundred dollars in one tap and my phone is literally throwing confetti at me.
The app is free so how does a free app cost me sixteen hundred dollars?
Plot twist.
By the end of this you'll know exactly who was paying for my free app and the one switch in the settings that saved my last four hundred dollars.
And most people click off before that part which is funny because the app really hopes you never find that switch.
So three months ago I put in two thousand dollars. My whole car fund. I buy one share of a company I've heard of and the screen explodes with confetti.
I'm a very smart investor so I picked the company because I liked their logo. That was my entire research.
And it feels amazing. Like I just won something. But all I did was press a button.
Then the notifications start. A stock is moving. Your watchlist is up. Don't miss out. And I tap and buy and sell and tap again.
Me at my desk every time my phone buzzes.
You know how people train a puppy? Click and treat and click and treat until the puppy sits before you even ask. I was the puppy and the confetti was the treat.
Every app wants to be a slot machine now and the confetti is the sound of a jackpot that never came.
Good boy Dave.
And this isn't just a joke. Massachusetts regulators accused one big trading app of exactly this and they had a fancy word for it. Gamification.
In their complaint one customer with zero experience made more than twelve thousand trades in about six months.
That guy's thumb after six months.
That app dropped the confetti later and paid seven and a half million dollars to settle. But puppy training works on everyone. Including me.
After one month I've made forty trades and my account is down ninety dollars. Which is weird because every trade was free. Right?
So I dig into the fine print. Why would a company build all this and charge me nothing?
Here's what I found. When I tap buy my order doesn't go straight to the stock exchange. The app sells it.
It sends my order to a giant trading firm called a wholesaler and the wholesaler pays the app for it. It's called payment for order flow.
Picture a taxi driver in a tourist town. A restaurant pays him ten dollars for every tourist he drops at its door. Is the food good? Doesn't matter. He gets paid when you walk in.
The taxi driver when you ask if the restaurant is good.
And the wholesaler makes money on the gap. It buys from me a little cheaper and sells a little higher. Like the money exchange booth at the airport.
Which means the app doesn't really care if I win. It cares that I trade. Like the popcorn guy at a football game. He doesn't care who scores.
The app watching me trade at two in the morning.

And there was one kind of trade that paid the app way more. Options. Quick guess. When I buy one options contract how much does the app get paid? A penny or a dollar or ten dollars? Write your guess in the comments.
So I tap the options button because my buddy at work swears it's how you turn two hundred dollars into two thousand.
My buddy explaining options.
An option is basically a coupon. It lets you buy a stock at a set price but only until a certain date. After that date the coupon expires.
Think of a half price pizza coupon. If pizza prices jump your coupon is gold. But if Friday midnight passes and you didn't use it it's just paper. And you paid for that paper.
So I buy coupons that bet a stock will jump this week. Four hundred dollars of them. The stock moves. Just not enough. Friday comes. Zero.
Me checking my options on Friday night.
My damage is now four hundred ninety dollars. And the app? It got paid the moment I bought those coupons. Win or lose.
So I asked a dangerous question. If the app gets paid every time then who exactly is paying it?
So I pull up the yearly report of the most famous free trading app. It's public and anyone can read it.
Last year that app made about four and a half billion dollars and one billion came from options alone.
Remember your guess? It's about forty eight cents per contract.
Wait. Forty eight cents? I lost four hundred dollars and they made forty eight cents?
Which sounds tiny. But tiny times millions of people like me every single day is a skyscraper.
Forty eight cents explained.
And who pays it? A small club of giant trading firms. And just three of them pay most of the money.
It's like a raccoon at a toll booth. He never left. He just got a faster computer.
The raccoon in twenty twenty six.
Is it illegal? No. In America it's legal and it's disclosed. Fans say it keeps trading free and critics say it pushes apps to make you trade more. Europe decided to ban it. Now you know how it works.
But I still believed one thing. At least my trades were free. And I was about to find out what free really costs.
I thought zero commission meant I paid nothing. Nope.
In twenty twenty the SEC said one big app gave its customers worse prices and those customers lost more than the commissions they saved. The app paid sixty five million dollars to settle.
And remember the airport money booth? Every time I buy and sell I cross that gap twice. And on the cheap weekly options small traders love that gap can eat more than ten percent.
Imagine buying a phone for one hundred dollars and the shop instantly offers to buy it back for eighty seven. Before you even open the box.
The phone shop guy.
One study found small traders lost about two billion dollars on options in less than two years. And paid even more in hidden costs on top.
Hidden costs every time I hit buy.
Two weeks later my damage hit one thousand dollars. And instead of stopping I did what almost everyone does. I tried to win it all back.
It's eleven at night. I have one thousand dollars left. My phone buzzes. A stock is moving fast.
And I think one big win and it's all back. So I put six hundred dollars on options that expire tomorrow. Tap. Confetti.
And here we are back at the start. Next day the coupons expire. Zero. Sixteen hundred dollars gone and four hundred left.
Me looking at my car fund.
So I wondered if I was just bad at this. Maybe there are people who are good at it. So I looked for proof.
I found a study from Brazil. Of the people who kept day trading for more than three hundred days ninety seven percent lost money.
Only about one in a hundred earned more than minimum wage. And the people didn't get better with practice.
Day traders after three hundred days of practice.
I felt like a puppy who just found out the treats were made of his own money. But there was one thing the app really didn't want me to find. A switch.
And honestly the worst feeling isn't losing the money. It's realizing the app knew I'd keep tapping before I did. They built the whole thing around the version of me at eleven at night.
Yeah whatever. Let's fix it.
So I open the settings. This is education and not advice.
Step one. In a lot of apps you can turn off options trading or ask support to remove it. I flip it off. No more coupons that melt on Friday.
Step two. Notifications off. No more clicker. The puppy gets to just be a dog again.
Step three. I move the app off my home screen. One extra swipe is a tiny wall that stops a lot of midnight taps.
Step four. Before any trade I ask one question. Would I still buy this with no confetti and no buzz? If the answer is no I close the app.
My thumb at midnight now.
Step five. For my long term money I set up a boring automatic investment every month into a low cost index fund. Boring is the point.
My portfolio now.
And my last four hundred dollars? Still there. But the best part wasn't the money. It was finally answering the question I started with.
So if the app is free who's paying?
I was.
Not with a fee I could see. With worse prices on every trade and coupons that melted on Friday and with my attention sold one tap at a time.
The app made forty eight cents on that contract and I lost six hundred dollars. Same tap.
The app and me after the same tap.
And the switch that saved my last four hundred dollars wasn't a secret trading trick. It was the off button for options. The one setting the confetti never mentioned.
So quick lessons. Free apps get paid when you trade and not when you win.
Options are coupons that expire and most small traders lose on them.
And confetti is a clicker. You're allowed to turn it off.
But my problems aren't over. Tonight a guy in a rented Lamborghini wants to teach me how to trade. I have four hundred dollars left and his course costs three hundred ninety nine.
Subscribe so you can watch me make a terrible decision. No confetti I promise.
